questions.prompt: For a standard-form linear program, the perturbed KKT system replaces complementary slackness by
questions.explanation: The primal equality, the dual equality, and the products \(x_i s_i = \mu\) are solved together. Ordinary complementarity is the limit \(\mu \to 0\). A sum \(x_i + s_i\) is a different equation. Negativity would leave the logarithmic neighborhood the iteration stays in. The dual equality still involves the cost.

questions.prompt: Take \(A = (1,\ 1)\), \(b = 6\), \(c = (4,\ 2)\), \(x = (4,\ 2)\), \(y = 0\), and \(s = (4,\ 2)\), with target \(\mu = 8\). The Newton step has \(d_x = (-2,\ 2)\). What is the new first primal coordinate, before any shortening?
questions.explanation: The point is primal feasible because \(4 + 2 = 6\), and dual feasible because \(s = c\). The products are \(16\) and \(4\). The Newton step that equalizes them at \(8\) is \(d_x = (-2,\ 2)\), with no change in \(y\) or \(s\). The new first coordinate is \(4 - 2 = 2\). The new point \((2,\ 4)\) has products \(8\) and \(8\). Reporting \(4\) keeps the old coordinate. Reporting \(-2\) is the step, not the updated coordinate. Reporting \(8\) is the target product.

questions.prompt: On the central path, the duality gap \(x^T s\) equals
questions.explanation: If every product \(x_i s_i\) equals \(\mu\), the sum of the products is \(n \mu\). That sum is the duality gap. Dividing by \(n\) would be the average product, which is \(\mu\), not the gap. The gap is zero only in the limit \(\mu \to 0\). The product of the norms is at least the absolute gap, and it equals the gap only in special alignments.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that drops at first and then flattens.
options: \(\lVert x\rVert \, \lVert s\rVert\), whether or not the products equal \(\mu\)

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order of one primal-dual iteration. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The Newton right-hand side contains the residuals, and the complementarity residual contains \(\mu\), so the target comes first. The step length is a fraction of a step that has already been computed. The update uses that shortened step. Reducing \(\mu\) for the next round happens after the point has moved. Shortening a step that has not been solved for is not a reordering of this list.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a segment</title><line x1="28" y1="150" x2="256" y2="150"/><polygon points="256,150 249.6,152.7 249.6,147.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="40" y1="164" x2="40" y2="20"/><polygon points="40,20 42.7,26.4 37.3,26.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="166" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="48" y="16" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="36" y1="132" x2="244" y2="36" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="70" y1="112" x2="190" y2="52" stroke-width="2.4"/><circle cx="70" cy="112" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="190" cy="52" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A solid segment joins two marked points on a dashed line.
steps: Choose a positive target \(\mu\) and form the primal, dual, and complementarity residuals at the current positive point.
Solve the Newton linear system on those residuals for the steps in \(x\), \(y\), and \(s\).
Shorten the common step length so the updated \(x\) and \(s\) stay positive.
Apply that shortened step, then reduce the target for the next round.

questions.prompt: A perturbed complementarity condition with target \(\mu = 4\) requires every product \(x_i s_i\) to equal \(4\). Which of these positive pairs \((x,\ s)\) satisfy it?
questions.explanation:
Each coordinate pair is checked on its own.
• \((2,\ 2)\) with \((2,\ 2)\) gives products \(4\) and \(4\).
• \((4,\ 1)\) with \((1,\ 4)\) gives products \(4\) and \(4\).
• \((4,\ 4)\) with \((1,\ 1)\) gives products \(4\) and \(4\).
• \((2,\ 4)\) with \((2,\ 2)\) gives products \(4\) and \(8\).
• \((4,\ 1)\) with \((1,\ 2)\) gives products \(4\) and \(2\).
A single matching product is not enough. Every product has to equal the target.

questions.prompt: One complementarity residual, for a primal coordinate \(x\), a slack \(s\), and a target \(m\), equals
questions.explanation: The perturbed equation is \(x s = m\), so the residual is \(x s - m\). Every name appears. The sum \(x + s - m\) is a different residual. The product \(x s\) alone is the complementarity value before the target is subtracted. Negating the product flips the sign of the Newton right-hand side.

questions.prompt: A note takes a Newton step on a perturbed system with \(x = (3,\ 1)\), \(s = (3,\ 1)\), \(b = 4\), \(c = (3,\ 1)\), \(y = 0\), and target \(\mu = 3\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The sums \(3 + 1 = 4\) and \(s = c\) make the primal and dual residuals zero. The products are \(9\) and \(1\), so the right-hand sides are \(-6\) and \(2\). Solving the Newton system gives \(d_x = (-2,\ 2)\) and no dual step. The update adds that step: \((3,\ 1) + (-2,\ 2) = (1,\ 3)\). Adding the opposite produces \((5,\ -1)\), which is not positive and is not the Newton update.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>two arrows from the origin</title><line x1="46" y1="161.7" x2="250" y2="161.7"/><polygon points="250,161.7 243.6,164.4 243.6,159" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="60.1" y1="176" x2="60.1" y2="28"/><polygon points="60.1,28 62.8,34.4 57.3,34.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="248" y="175.7" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="66.1" y="30" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="60.1" y1="161.7" x2="235.9" y2="138.9"/><polygon points="235.9,138.9 229.9,142.5 229.2,137.1" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="243.9" y="130.9" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">u</text><line x1="60.1" y1="161.7" x2="118.7" y2="42.3"/><polygon points="118.7,42.3 118.3,49.3 113.4,46.9" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="126.7" y="34.3" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">v</text></svg>
steps: The primal residual and the dual residual are both zero.
The complementarity right-hand sides \(\mu - x_i s_i\) are \(3 - 9 = -6\) and \(3 - 1 = 2\).
The Newton update adds the opposite of \(d_x\), so the new primal vector is \((5,\ -1)\).
reasons: The step \(d_x\) is added. The new primal vector is \((1,\ 3)\), not \((5,\ -1)\).

questions.prompt: After the Newton step of the feasible point \(x = (4,\ 2)\), \(s = (4,\ 2)\) with target \(\mu = 8\), the new primal vector is \((2,\ 4)\) and the slacks are unchanged. What is the new duality gap \(x^T s\)?
questions.explanation: The new products are \(2 \cdot 4 = 8\) and \(4 \cdot 2 = 8\). Their sum is \(16\). That is \(n \mu\) with \(n = 2\). The old gap was \(16 + 4 = 20\). Reporting \(8\) is one product, not the sum. Reporting \(20\) is the old gap. Reporting \(4\) is a coordinate. On the central path the gap equals the sum of the products, which the Newton step has just equalized.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that drops at first and then flattens.

questions.explanation: The perturbed map is nonlinear because of the products \(x_i s_i\). Newton's method linearizes it. A full step can drive a coordinate negative, so the step is shortened. A vertex pivot is the simplex method. Setting \(\mu = 0\) is the predictor, or affine-scaling, direction. The centering target stays positive on a path-following step. The step updates \(x\), \(y\), and \(s\) together.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a segment</title><line x1="28" y1="150" x2="256" y2="150"/><polygon points="256,150 249.6,152.7 249.6,147.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="40" y1="164" x2="40" y2="20"/><polygon points="40,20 42.7,26.4 37.3,26.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="166" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="48" y="16" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="36" y1="132" x2="244" y2="36" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="70" y1="112" x2="190" y2="52" stroke-width="2.4"/><circle cx="70" cy="112" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="190" cy="52" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/></svg>

options: takes a Newton step on the perturbed KKT map, then shortens it so \(x\) and \(s\) stay positive
pivots from one vertex to another

questions.prompt: Driving the target \(\mu\) toward \(0\) along the central path makes
questions.explanation: On the path every product equals \(\mu\), so the gap \(n \mu\) tends to \(0\) with the target. The path is defined to keep \(A x = b\) and the dual equality, so those residuals stay zero. The points stay positive for every positive \(\mu\). The Jacobian carries the diagonal matrices of \(x\) and \(s\), but also the constraint matrix \(A\), so it is not diagonal in general.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls toward the horizontal axis.
options: the complementarity products, and therefore the duality gap, tend to \(0\)
the primal residual \(A x - b\) grow
the iterates leave the positive orthant on the first step
the Newton Jacobian diagonal for every linear program

questions.prompt: A central point of a standard-form linear program in \(n = 5\) variables has every product \(x_i s_i\) equal to \(2\). What is the duality gap?
questions.explanation: The gap is the sum of the products, which is \(n \mu = 5 \cdot 2 = 10\). Reporting \(2\) is the common product. Reporting \(5\) is the variable count. Reporting \(2.5\) divides the product by the count instead of multiplying. The gap is the quantity the target \(\mu\) controls. It is not the distance from the current point to a vertex.

questions.prompt: A short-step path-following method reaches a duality gap that is a fraction \(\varepsilon\) of the initial gap in a number of Newton steps on the order of
questions.explanation: The classical short-step count is a bound on how many Newton steps it takes to shrink the duality gap. The gap, not the Euclidean distance to a vertex, is the quantity inside \(\varepsilon\). A simplex pivot count is a different algorithm and can be exponential. The count grows, slowly, with the number of inequalities and with the requested reduction. The condition number of \(A\) is not the quantity this iteration bound tracks.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls toward the horizontal axis.
options: \(n\) simplex pivots, with no dependence on the gap
a constant that does not grow with \(n\) or with \(1/\varepsilon\)
the square of the condition number of \(A\), with no role for the gap
